analysis.one_liner: Lets people injured by pesticides sue the pesticide's manufacturer in federal court.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let people sue pesticide makers in federal court for injuries, has had no action since a July 2025 Senate committee referral, with a single Democratic cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write a new right into federal pesticide law: anyone whose body or property is hurt by a pesticide could sue the company that registered it in federal court, seeking compensatory and punitive damages. It would also make clear that injured people keep whatever claims they already have under state law. The bill was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee in July 2025 and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to pesticides — farmworkers and their families, people living near sprayed fields, and owners of crops, livestock, or property damaged by drift — would gain a direct route to federal court against the pesticide's registrant, a route federal pesticide law does not currently provide. They could seek both compensatory and punitive damages, and their existing state-law claims would stay intact.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a private right of action: any person whose person or property is injured by a pesticide may sue the pesticide's registrant for monetary damages in federal district court, a remedy the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act does not currently give individuals.

Allows courts, at their discretion, to award both compensatory damages (paying for the actual injury) and punitive damages (extra amounts meant to punish and deter), which raises the stakes for manufacturers that injure people.
Includes an express non-preemption clause stating that nothing in the new federal right overrides state law claims, so injured people can pursue whichever forum gives them the better case.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide registrants — the chemical companies that hold federal registrations for pesticide products — would bear new litigation exposure, including potential punitive damages, whenever their products injure people or property. Those costs could be passed on in pesticide prices or lead companies to pull products from the market.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not allow recovery of attorney's fees or court costs. Under the American rule, each side pays its own lawyers, so a person with a real but expensive-to-prove injury could win damages yet still walk away owing their own legal bills — and lawyers may decline strong cases they would take if fees were available.

Suits may be brought only against the registrant — the company that holds the federal registration — not against applicators or other parties in the chain who may have actually caused the exposure, and punitive damages are available only at the court's discretion, making outcomes less predictable.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost side: broader litigation exposure for pesticide makers could raise prices for farmers or cause some products to be withdrawn, which would land on the agriculture economy those same rural communities depend on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — giving injured people a direct federal lawsuit against pesticide manufacturers, where federal law currently offers none — is a genuine accountability tool for farmworkers and rural residents, and the non-preemption clause is well designed because it preserves rather than narrows existing rights. But the bill is weakened by its own drafting: barring recovery of attorney's fees makes it much harder for ordinary plaintiffs to actually enforce the right it creates. It is a modest, targeted bill whose main weakness is that it may be practically difficult to use.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee in July 2025, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Pesticide Injury Accountability Act of 2025 in the Senate on July 17, 2025.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry — the standard first step that sends a bill to the committee with jurisdiction over it.
The full action history shows nothing after the referral: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote. One Senate Democrat has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers are better off so far: because the bill has not moved, they face no new federal litigation exposure. People harmed by pesticides are no worse off than before, but they have gained nothing either.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and has been its only active sponsor.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 17, 2025 and has taken no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken, so the partisan split is untested, but the bill's only support so far is Democratic: Senator Booker and one other Senate Democrat, with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would expose registrants — the chemical companies holding federal pesticide registrations — to federal lawsuits by anyone their products injure, including punitive damages, an exposure federal pesticide law does not currently allow. The bill has not advanced, so that exposure has not materialized.

Farmers whose crops, livestock, or property are damaged by pesticide drift would gain a new way to recover damages, but if manufacturers face more litigation they could raise prices or withdraw products that farmers rely on for pest control.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress runs through early January 2027, so the bill is technically alive. But the great majority of Senate bills referred to committee never receive a hearing or a vote, and this one has sat untouched since July 2025 with a single cosponsor and no committee activity. Unless it picks up substantial additional support or is attached to a larger agriculture or farm bill package, it is likely to die quietly when this Congress ends.
